trial_name: IABP-SHOCK II — Intraaortic Balloon Support for Myocardial Infarction with Cardiogenic Shock (2012)
journal: The New England Journal of Medicine
citation: Thiele H, Zeymer U, Neumann FJ, Ferenc M, Olbrich HG, Hausleiter J, et al. Intraaortic balloon support for myocardial infarction with cardiogenic shock. N Engl J Med. 2012;367(14):1287-1296.
one_liner: Routine IABP does not reduce 30-day mortality in AMI-related cardiogenic shock treated with early revascularisation.

pico.population: Adults with STEMI or NSTEMI complicated by cardiogenic shock and planned early revascularisation (predominantly PCI)
pico.intervention: IABP inserted via femoral access before or immediately after revascularisation, continued until haemodynamic stabilisation (median 3 days)
pico.comparison: No planned IABP (standard care including early revascularisation, vasoactive support, ventilation; rescue IABP permitted)

background.existing_knowledge: Cardiogenic shock complicating AMI carries persistently high early mortality despite contemporary revascularisation and intensive care.
background.knowledge_gap: IABP was widely used as adjunctive support in AMI-related shock, but outcome benefit was uncertain and vascular/bleeding risks existed.
background.hypothesis: Routine IABP support reduces 30-day all-cause mortality compared with no planned IABP in patients with AMI complicated by cardiogenic shock undergoing early revascularisation.

methods.design: Prospective, multicentre, randomised, open-label, parallel-group controlled trial; 1:1 central internet-based randomisation stratified by centre; 37 centres in Germany; enrolment June 2009 to March 2012.
methods.setting: 37 centres in Germany, high-resource ICUs with rapid PCI access.

inclusion: Adults (≥18 years) with STEMI or non-STEMI complicated by cardiogenic shock
Intention to pursue early revascularisation (predominantly PCI)

Cardiogenic shock defined as: systolic BP <90 mmHg for ≥30 min or catecholamine therapy to maintain systolic BP ≥90 mmHg, plus pulmonary congestion, plus signs of impaired organ perfusion (altered mental status, cold/clammy skin, oliguria <30 mL/h, or serum lactate >2.0 mmol/L)
exclusion: Mechanical causes of shock (e.g., acute severe mitral regurgitation, ventricular septal rupture)
Severe peripheral artery disease precluding IABP

methods.intervention: IABP inserted via femoral access before or immediately after revascularisation, providing counterpulsation support (typically 1:1 ECG triggering) until sustained haemodynamic stabilisation; weaning by stepwise reduction of trigger ratio. Delivered IABP support duration: median 3.0 days (IQR 2.0–4.0; range 1–16 days) among those treated with IABP.
methods.comparison: No planned IABP (standard care including early revascularisation, vasoactive support, ventilation and other organ support as required); IABP permitted as rescue (e.g., for mechanical complications or clinical deterioration).
methods.blinding: Open-label to treating teams and participants; primary endpoint (mortality) objective; clinical endpoint adjudication committee blinded to treatment assignment.
methods.sample_size_power: Planned sample size 600 (300/group); powered (80%) to detect a 12 percentage-point absolute increase in 30-day survival (assumed 56% control vs 68% IABP) with overall type I error 0.05 and final analysis significance threshold 0.044.
secondary_outcomes: Life-threatening or severe bleeding (GUSTO) in hospital
methods.follow_up: 30 days for primary endpoint; longer-term follow-up reported in later publications (12 months, 6 years).

headline_bullets: Routine IABP did not reduce 30-day mortality vs control (39.7% vs 41.3%; RR 0.96; 95% CI 0.79–1.17; P=0.69).
Key process-of-care measures (time to stabilisation, catecholamine duration, ICU stay, ventilation) were similar between groups despite substantial IABP exposure.
Major safety outcomes (stroke, severe bleeding, limb ischaemia) were not significantly different.
Subgroup analyses were broadly consistent; nominal interactions for prior MI and hypertension were likely chance findings.

outcomes_table.note: Primary analysis sample 598 (1 consent withdrawal, 1 lost to follow-up)

outcomes_table.outcome: Life-threatening or severe bleeding in hospital (GUSTO)
Duration of intensive care treatment (days; median [IQR])

outcomes_table.note: Process-of-care endpoint; denominators reflect available data
Rescue mechanical support use differed between groups

subgroup_table.note: Nominal interaction; IABP possibly harmful in this subgroup

safety: Reinfarction: 3.0% IABP vs 1.3% control (RR 2.24, 95% CI 0.70–7.18, P=0.16)
Peripheral ischaemic complications requiring intervention: 4.3% vs 3.4% (RR 1.29, 95% CI 0.58–2.90, P=0.53)

domains.notes: Central internet-based randomisation (1:1), stratified by centre; baseline characteristics closely balanced (age median 70 vs 69 years; LVEF median 35% vs 35%).
Open-label design; potential for differential co-interventions, but primary endpoint (mortality) is objective and endpoint adjudication committee was blinded.
Primary analysis included 598/600 (99.7%) due to one withdrawal of consent and one lost to follow-up; minimal attrition. Per-protocol analysis consistent with ITT.
IABP received by 95.7% of IABP group; 4.3% did not receive IABP. Crossover to IABP in 10.0% of controls. Delivered IABP duration median 3.0 days (IQR 2.0–4.0).
Revascularisation rates high (PCI 95.8%, CABG 3.7%). LVAD implantation more frequent in control group (7.7% vs 3.3%, P=0.02), potentially diluting treatment effect.
Multicentre (37 centres) increases generalisability; treatment effects directionally similar across most subgroups.
IABP inserted before or immediately after PCI; median support 3 days. Mortality similar whether insertion before vs after revascularisation.
Prespecified sequential monitoring with conservative final alpha (0.044); near-complete primary endpoint dataset; supportive analyses did not change inference.

internal_validity.verdict: Overall internal validity is moderate-to-strong: robust randomisation and follow-up with an objective primary endpoint, but open-label design, clinically driven crossovers (10% of controls), and differential rescue mechanical support introduce plausible dilution and co-intervention effects.

domains.notes: Broad AMI-related cardiogenic shock population (STEMI and NSTEMI), typical age (~70 years), high pre-randomisation resuscitation rates (~43%). Exclusions (shock >12 h, prolonged resuscitation, mechanical complications, severe PVD, age >90) limit applicability to very late presenters, profound anoxic injury, or mechanical causes.

Highly applicable to high-resource systems with rapid PCI and intensive care. Extrapolation to settings without timely revascularisation or to contemporary practice dominated by more potent MCS (microaxial pumps, VA-ECMO) should be cautious.

Findings apply to conventional IABP counterpulsation as routinely delivered in a modern PCI-era shock pathway; they do not directly address other mechanical support devices or non-AMI shock phenotypes.

external_validity.verdict: External validity is good for AMI-related cardiogenic shock managed with early PCI in advanced centres, but is limited for non-AMI shock, mechanical complications, late shock, prolonged arrest, and settings without timely revascularisation or access to escalation therapies.

strengths: Large, contemporary randomised trial in a high-mortality population
Objective primary endpoint with near-complete follow-up
High revascularisation rates reflecting modern care
Prespecified sequential monitoring and supportive analyses
limitations: Open-label design with clinically mandated crossovers and protocol deviations
Potential dilution by differential rescue mechanical support (higher LVAD use in controls)
Powered for a relatively large absolute mortality difference (smaller benefits/harm cannot be excluded)
Results pertain to IABP (modest haemodynamic augmentation) rather than more potent mechanical support strategies

critical_appraisal.summary: IABP-SHOCK II is a well-conducted RCT with robust randomisation and near-complete follow-up, but open-label design and differential rescue therapy may dilute effect; overall moderate internal validity and good external validity for PCI-era AMI shock.
strengths: Central randomisation, objective primary endpoint, near-complete follow-up
High revascularisation rates reflecting modern care
weaknesses: Differential rescue LVAD use may dilute effect
Powered for large effect; smaller benefits not excluded

sections.authors_conclusion: Routine IABP does not improve 30-day survival or process-of-care measures in AMI-related cardiogenic shock treated with early revascularisation, and should not be used routinely.

clinical_bottom_line.verdict: Routine IABP should not be used in AMI-related cardiogenic shock; it does not reduce mortality.
clinical_bottom_line.applies_to: Patients with AMI-related cardiogenic shock undergoing early revascularisation (PCI) in high-resource settings.
clinical_bottom_line.does_not_mean: IABP is harmful; it may still have a role in mechanical complications or as a bridge to more advanced support.
implementation_caveats: Reserve IABP for selected indications (e.g., mechanical complications, bridging) rather than routine use.
Consider more potent mechanical support strategies in refractory shock.

controversies.notes: IABP provides modest haemodynamic augmentation; in AMI shock treated with early PCI and vasoactive support, this degree of support may be insufficient to alter mortality despite physiological plausibility.

controversies.topic: Crossover and rescue therapy as diluters
controversies.notes: Control crossover to IABP (10%) and higher LVAD use in controls (7.7% vs 3.3%) could dilute a true treatment effect; however, per-protocol and adjusted analyses remained neutral, supporting a genuinely small/absent mortality benefit.
Nominal subgroup interactions (e.g., prior MI and hypertension) did not provide a coherent, practice-changing phenotype and are compatible with chance findings given multiple comparisons.
Subsequent publications at 12 months and at 6 years reported no survival advantage with routine IABP, reinforcing the early neutral result.
Systematic reviews and meta-analyses incorporating IABP-SHOCK II show no mortality reduction for IABP in AMI-related cardiogenic shock in the contemporary era, aligning with the trial’s conclusions.
Major society guidance has moved away from routine IABP use in AMI-related cardiogenic shock, reflecting the evidence base consolidated by IABP-SHOCK II and subsequent syntheses/statements.

unresolved_questions: Is there a subgroup of AMI shock patients who benefit from IABP (e.g., based on timing, haemodynamic profile, or revascularisation completeness)?
What is the role of more potent mechanical circulatory support (microaxial pumps, VA-ECMO) in AMI shock, and how should they be selected?
Does timing of IABP insertion (before vs after PCI) influence outcomes in specific scenarios?
Can better risk stratification identify patients who might benefit from IABP as a bridge to recovery or advanced support?

quick_recall.one_line_takeaway: Routine IABP does not reduce 30-day mortality in AMI-related cardiogenic shock treated with early revascularisation.
